item.title: Showa Daibutsu (Seiryuji): Japan's Tallest Bronze Buddha — Guide
item.description: Just outside Aomori City, the tranquil temple of Seiryuji is home to the Showa Daibutsu — at 21.35 metres, Japan’s tallest seated bronze Great Buddha, taller even than the famous Buddhas of Nara and Kamakura. Cast in 1984, it presides over spacious grounds with a striking five-story pagoda. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Aomori City, Aomori Hours ~9:00–17:30 (seasonal) Admission Around ¥500 Time needed About 1 hour Best time Year-round; autumn colours fine What to See The 21 m bronze Great Buddha, Japan’s tallest seated bronze figure.

item.title: Kinkaku-ji Guide: Kyoto's Golden Pavilion
item.description: A three-storey pavilion covered in pure gold leaf, mirrored perfectly in the still pond before it, framed by pines and — if you’re lucky — dusted with snow or backed by autumn maples: Kinkaku-ji is the postcard image of Kyoto, and one of the few sights that genuinely lives up to it. The Golden Pavilion shimmers whether under bright sun, soft cloud, or a rare winter snowfall, and the moment you round the path and it appears across the water is unforgettable.

item.title: Kiyomizu-dera Guide: The Temple on Stilts Above Kyoto
item.description: Perched on the wooded slopes of Higashiyama, Kiyomizu-dera juts out over the hillside on a vast wooden stage held up by enormous pillars — built, famously, without a single nail. From the stage you look out over a sea of maple and cherry trees to the rooftops of Kyoto beyond. It is one of Japan’s most beloved temples, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the climax of the most atmospheric temple approach in the city: the stone-paved, shop-lined slopes of Sannenzaka and Ninenzaka.

item.title: Mount Oyama Guide: Cable Car, Afuri Shrine & Access
item.description: Rising at the eastern edge of the Tanzawa range, Mount Oyama (1,252 m) has been a place of worship and pilgrimage for centuries — and today it’s one of the most accessible and rewarding half-day mountains near Tokyo. A nostalgic shopping street of tofu restaurants and inns leads to a cable car that climbs to Afuri Shrine, with sweeping views over the Kanto Plain and, on clear days, the sea and Mt.

item.title: Narita-san Shinshoji Temple Guide: Access from the Airport & Tips
item.description: Just minutes from Narita Airport, Narita-san Shinshoji Temple is one of the most important and atmospheric Buddhist temples in the Tokyo area — the perfect first or last stop on a trip to Japan. Founded in 940 and headquarters of the Shingon Chisan sect, it enshrines Fudo Myo-o, the fierce, flame-wreathed guardian deity, and draws millions of worshippers a year (it ranks among Japan’s busiest for New Year’s visits). Spread across a hillside of grand halls, a soaring pagoda and a tranquil landscaped park, and approached by a charming old street of eel restaurants and souvenir shops, it offers a deep dose of living Japanese tradition right by the airport.

item.title: Senso-ji Temple Guide: Asakusa's Ancient Heart from Dawn to Dusk
item.description: Senso-ji is the oldest and most visited temple in Tokyo — but it is also one of the most misunderstood. Millions of visitors pass through the Kaminarimon gate, photograph the giant paper lantern, browse a few stalls on Nakamise-dori, and leave in 20 minutes. Those who stay longer, arrive earlier, or return in the evening discover something different entirely: a living place of worship with 1,400 years of continuous practice, where the incense smoke carries real prayers, and where the early morning light through the five-storey pagoda is among the most beautiful sights in the city.
